prize_parts.citation: For the development of ionizable lipid nanoparticles, self-assembled carriers whose pH-dependent charge and lipid phase behaviour enable nucleic-acid medicines to be encapsulated, circulate and be released inside cells

statement.case_for: My position is unchanged after round 1. The chair asks which discovery the citation honours. It is the formation and design principle of the carrier: nucleic acid is entrapped within a lipid particle through self-assembly, using a lipid whose charge is switched by pH, so that the particle is close to neutral in blood and becomes cationic in the acidic endosome, where bilayer-to-non-bilayer phase behaviour drives membrane fusion and release. That is physical chemistry of self-assembled matter, and a non-specialist can follow it as 'a lipid that changes charge with acidity, so medicines can be packed in and delivered into cells'. It does not rest on the mRNA cargo, so the 2023 Medicine prize for nucleoside modification is a different achievement; the citation should name the carrier and not the vaccines. No other shortlisted candidate combines this conceptual clarity with consequences that are already independently proven in patients (an approved siRNA drug and the mRNA vaccines). Cullis, Madden and Hope are the people I can tie to the encapsulation and lipid-phase principle on which every later ionizable-lipid optimisation builds; that is the part I would reward as chemistry.
statement.case_against: The credit problem is real and round 1 has made it sharper: Aili moved to my trio, but Linke, Somfai, Aqvist and Zou point to MacLachlan, Anderson and Langer, and three different trios across the committee do suggest that credit is unsettled. If the committee decides that the decisive step was clinical siRNA delivery or combinatorial lipid discovery, my trio is the wrong one, and my knowledge of who did which step comes from memory, not from the files. A second objection is that a majority may regard this as formulation, not chemistry, in which case the configuration cannot reach five votes. I also have to keep in mind that I am a lipid physical chemist and may overweight the self-assembly perspective.

responses.point: Linke accepts the chemistry framing if the citation is built on lipid phase behaviour and ionizable-lipid design, but doubts that Cullis, Madden and Hope capture the decisive step, naming MacLachlan for siRNA delivery and Anderson for combinatorial lipid discovery, and he asks whether the prize honours the physical chemistry or the delivery systems.
responses.response: That is the right question and my answer is the physical chemistry: the principle of pH-controlled charge and lipid polymorphism that makes a self-assembled particle load, circulate and release. Later siRNA optimisation and library screening refined that principle and mattered a great deal clinically, but they build on it, and I would argue that a chemistry citation should sit on the principle. I accept that this is a judgement and not a fact, and that if you weight the clinically decisive optimisation, MacLachlan would enter. I would still rather reward the origin of the design logic than the screening that tuned it. I note that your own B027 trio has the same difficulty with Ciulli, so crowded credit is not unique to B062.

responses.point: Aqvist doubts that lipid nanoparticles are a chemistry game-changer because much of the contribution is formulation, the allocation among six names is unstable, and the 2023 Medicine prize overlaps.
responses.response: I think the distinction between formulation and design is where we differ. A formulation tweak is an empirical adjustment of a mixture; here a molecular property, the pKa of the lipid headgroup, was chosen so that the particle changes behaviour at endosomal pH, and phase behaviour explains why release works. That is a design rule and not a recipe. On the overlap, I agree that the citation must say it concerns the carrier. On allocation I concede the point is open, and I would like to know whether you would support B062 if the committee agreed on the names, or whether your objection is to the chemistry itself.

responses.point: Somfai says that when three members propose three different laureate sets for the same discovery, attribution is not settled enough to carry a prize, even though he accepts the physical-chemistry framing.
responses.response: The signal is fair, but the divergence has narrowed in discussion: Aili has moved to Cullis, Madden and Hope, so two members now share the same three, and the remaining disagreement is about whether to credit the early principle or the later optimisation, which is a question of what the prize honours, not of who did the work. I do not think that is equivalent to unsettled facts, but I agree that it is harder than your two-name Buchwald-Hartwig attribution, and I do not want to treat a clean attribution as stronger science. I also still hold that B019 extends a concept honoured in 2010, while B062 is a new area for the prize.

responses.point: Chabes pairs base editing with a two-name B027 and ranks condensates (B050) below both because many cellular condensate claims rest on overexpression and imaging and lack independent quantitative reproduction.
responses.response: On condensates I accept the evidence argument and it has moved B050 further behind B062 in my own ordering; I keep it only as an alternative because the multivalency framework is sound in vitro. On your two-part structure, I would not support combining unrelated achievements to build a majority, since that reflects the three-person cap more than the science. If the committee does pair parts, I would want each part to stand on its own merits, and I am not persuaded that dropping Deshaies from B027 helps the case.

responses.point: Brzezinski moved to B027 because the mechanism is documented, independently confirmed and easier to evaluate, and regards condensate maturity as a stronger objection than the open questions around degraders.
responses.response: I agree that the maturity of condensates is the weaker case this year and that B027 has the most support, which I take seriously as information about the committee, though not as a substitute for the science. My difficulty with B027 remains the one the chair raises: PROTACs and cereblon-based glues were discovered by different groups at different times, and there is still no approved degrader to give independent proof of the principle. Lipid nanoparticles have that proof already. I would accept B027 as the committee's choice if the citation were kept to the E3 recruitment principle, but it is not my preferred configuration.

uncertainties: Whether the committee wants the citation to honour the early encapsulation and ionizable-lipid principle (Cullis, Madden, Hope) or later siRNA delivery and library discovery (MacLachlan, Anderson, Langer); my account of who did what is from memory and unverified.
Whether a majority will accept lipid nanoparticles as chemistry rather than formulation, and whether the 2023 Medicine prize can be kept clearly separate in the wording.
Whether B027 will turn out to be the only configuration that can reach five votes despite the absence of an approved degrader and the crowded credit.
Whether the evidence on functional biomolecular condensates (B050) will mature enough to rival B062 in a later year.
statement.conflict_note: Lipid self-assembly and membranes are my own research area, which makes me scientifically close to B062 and B050; I have no personal, collaborative or institutional tie to any credited person that is apparent from my profile. I am a Lund colleague of Linke and Somfai, which has no bearing on the candidates. No recusal issue is apparent, and nothing in round 1 has changed this.
